title: KV cache: reuse, eviction, paging & memory bandwidth investigation
body:
Summary:

This is a working note for our KV cache investigation focused on reuse rates, eviction behaviour, paging to host, and memory-bandwidth interactions. The goal is to understand latency outliers and token-cost tradeoffs for long-context workloads and to propose short-term mitigations plus follow-up experiments.

High-level findings (TL;DR):
- KV reuse depends heavily on workload type: chat-like session workloads show 70–90% reuse for active prefixes, while single-turn long-context inference has reuse < 30% for worst-case.
- Eviction spikes correlate with bursts of long sequences + high concurrency; LRU-based eviction currently causes repeat recomputation for partially overlapping sequences.
- We observed paging to host (PCIe transfers) during memory-pressure experiments; sustained PCIe transfer rates of ~8–18 GB/s caused tail latency spikes (~30–120 ms extra per request).
- GPU HBM utilization peaked at ~75–92% in heavy-kv scenarios; memory-bandwidth is a dominant bottleneck for KV-heavy attention when sequence lengths exceed 2k and batch size >= 8.

Context / motivation:
- Customers pushing 4k+ contexts and multi-turn chat have seen latency variability and higher per-token cost. We suspect KV cache management (reuse/eviction/paging) is a primary contributor.
- This doc contains profiling notes, micro-benchmark results, and concrete experiments to reduce latency tail and unit cost.

Test environment / setup:
- Hardware: 8x A100-40GB per node (single node tests for profiling), PCIe Gen4 interconnect for host paging tests.
- Runtime: serving-runtime main@commit 8f9c51a (including recent KV-allocator changes).
- Model: LLaMA-2-13B (fp16 baseline), 32-layer, hidden=4096.
- Benchmarks: synthetic traces and sampled production traces (anonymized):
  - chat-session trace: avg seq growth 64 tokens/request, median session length 28 requests
  - long-doc trace: single request seq lengths {512, 2048, 4096}
- Instrumentation: nvprof/nvtx markers, NVML sampling for GPU memory BW, custom runtime traces for KV allocations/evictions, per-request latency histograms (p50/p95/p99).

Key metrics we collected (representative numbers):
- KV reuse rate (fraction of KV keys reused between consecutive requests in same session):
  - chat-session (batch=1): median 82%, p10 60%, p90 92%
  - chat-session (batch=8): median 74%, p10 52%, p90 88%
  - long-doc 2048 (batch=1): median 27%
  - long-doc 4096 (batch=1): median 12%
- Eviction events (evictions per 1000 requests, LRU policy, cache size=48GB):
  - chat-session (batch=1): 4 evictions / 1k reqs
  - concurrent bursts (batch=32, mixed seq): 112 evictions / 1k reqs (hotspots)
- Paging to host (when total KV > HBM and allocator starts host paging):
  - Observed PCIe transfer rates: sustained 8–18 GB/s during heavy page-in activity
  - Latency impact: 95th pct tail increased by 30–120 ms correlated with page-in windows
- GPU HBM bandwidth (measured via NVML):
  - baseline (short seqs): 420–680 GB/s sustained
  - heavy-kv (seq >= 2k, batched): 920–1180 GB/s sustained at peaks (close to device max on A100 variants)
  - overall memory pressure correlated with increased kernel stalls and higher SM idle due to memory stalls

Profiling notes / observations:
- Kernel-level hotspots: KV read/write kernels and attention KV update kernels dominate when reuse < 50%. The attention compute kernels are still heavy, but the incremental overhead of reloading KV from host or from evicted blocks is reflected in extra memcpy/synchronization time.
- Eviction thrashing: LRU evicts KV slices that are still needed by near-future requests (common in chat where users frequently request context windows that partially overlap). This causes recompute and increased memory traffic.
- Paging pattern: when total working set slightly exceeds HBM capacity, we see periodic page-in spikes rather than continuous streaming; this suggests our allocator/page policy moves chunks eagerly during peaks, which amplifies tail latency.
- Batching effect: larger batch sizes increase aggregate working set (sum of active KV per batch) and lead to both higher HBM bandwidth and more frequent evictions. However, batching improves GPU compute throughput; we need a better sweet spot for latency-sensitive workloads.

Microbenchmarks performed:
- Controlled reuse test: fixed context prefixes with variable overlap (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%) across requests to measure reuse vs latency. Results: latency scales inversely with reuse; >75% reuse gives near-baseline latency, <25% reuse increases per-request latency by 30–80%.
- Eviction policy comparison (LRU vs segmented-LRU vs frequency-aware): small-scale run (cache=48GB) showed seg-LRU reduced evictions by ~28% on chat trace and p99 latency by ~18% vs plain LRU. LFU-like policies reduced recompute for repetitive tokens but suffered cold-start overhead.
- Host-paging stress: forced working set to 1.3x HBM capacity. Observed heavy PCIe transfers and p99 latency spikes. Sequential page-in of large KV slices (>= 32MB) causes longer blocking periods.

Initial conclusions:
1) Memory bandwidth is a first-order bottleneck for KV-heavy workloads: when reuse is low and batch sizes are moderate/high, we saturate HBM and see kernel stalls.
2) Eviction policy matters: naive LRU leads to repeated recomputation for partially overlapping contexts. A policy that considers temporal locality at segment granularity reduces thrash.
3) Paging to host is expensive and non-linear in latency impact: small amounts of host paging lead to disproportionate tail latency increases due to synchronous page-ins.

Immediate mitigation ideas (short-term, low risk):
- Increase cache granularity: allocate KV in smaller segments (e.g., 16KB-256KB) so eviction is finer-grained, reducing unnecessary evictions of hot subsections.
- Segmented LRU: implement a hot/long-lived segment promotion to reduce eviction of repeatedly used KV slices.
- Conservative host paging threshold: avoid paging until >1.2x HBM or implement background asynchronous prefetching for predicted upcoming KV slices (based on session history).
- Adaptive batching guidance: for latency-sensitive routes, cap effective batch size or prefer accumulation windows that respect KV working set budgets.

Follow-up experiments (medium term):
- Run a full A/B comparing LRU vs seg-LRU in Dedicated and Hosted with production-like traffic for 72h; track p50/p95/p99 latency and token cost.
- Implement async paging + prefetch using session-prediction heuristics and measure impact on p99 latency under >HBM workloads.
- Try hybrid eviction that factors in reuse probability (learned model) for hot sessions.

Action items / owners:
- Marcus Li: prototype segmented-LRU allocator + unit tests (due: 2026-03-25)
- Priya Shah: schedule 72h A/B on dedicated cluster with chat-production trace (due: 2026-04-01)
- Elena Gomez: add NVTX markers for finer-grained page-in tracing and add background telemetry for PCIe traffic (due: 2026-03-22)
- Alex Chen (me): coordinate rollout plan and prepare canary evaluation template for Console (due: 2026-03-30)

Open questions / notes to investigate:
- Can we exploit prefix similarity hashing to keep only a small fingerprint index in HBM and lazily rebuild KV blocks on demand? Tradeoffs need measurement.
- How much benefit does model-specific KV packing (reordering KV layout by attention head / layer importance) yield?
- Is there an opportunity to offload cold KV storage to a fast NVMe pool with a dedicated DMA engine to reduce PCIe stall impact?

Appendix: representative command snippets used for profiling:
- NVML sampling: python tools/gpu_sample.py --interval 0.1 --metrics gpu_memory_bw,sm_util,mem_used
- Runtime trace collection: SGX_TRACE=1 ./serving-runtime --trace-kv --trace-alloc > kv-trace.log
- Eviction simulation harness: tools/kv_eviction_sim --policy lru --cache-gb 48 --trace samples/chat_trace.json

Notes: this is a working doc; numbers are representative from runs on the test cluster and may vary on other hardware and software commits. Please add observations / counterexamples below or in the linked Slack thread.
